You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 0.76 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal (weak); Ip = 12 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 12 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 6800 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 22000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weakest excitation; Ip = 8 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 22000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 10 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 12 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       0.56   0.566    11.6       -    0.0314  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S2      0.558   0.563    11.2       -    0.0457  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       2.24    2.26    35.4   0.329     0.228  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S4      0.334   0.339    8.95       -   0.00508  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S5      0.573   0.581    15.7       -    0.0329  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S6      0.459   0.462     6.1       -    0.0211  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 3 of 12.

RESULTS OF YOUR PREVIOUS ROUND:

Design 1 's_sshi_transfer': failed the screen and was not tuned (topology 3bac4780943e).
L1 L pzp n1 0.0047
S1 S n1 pzn ctrl=G1
G1 SYNC ton=3.4e-05s phase=0 edges=both
D1 D pzp n2 DSCH
D2 D pzn n2 DSCH

G2 SYNC ton=0.0001s phase=0.1 edges=both

DZ1 D 0 out DZ33
screen (out fixed at 1.8 V): S2: -1.8 uW of 0.476 uW needed (-377 %); S4: -1.8 uW of 0.147 uW needed (-1220 %); S6: -1.8 uW of 0.324 uW needed (-555 %)
what this means:
- with the output fixed at 1.8 V, the net power delivered covers only -377 % of the load's need on S2 (heavy load), -1220 % of the load's need on S4 (weakest excitation), -555 % of the load's need on S6 (Cp +20 %, hot) (best of the value presets tried)

REPEATED PROBLEM: your last three designs all show the same failure: too little power reaches the output on some conditions [underpower]. Change the part of the circuit responsible for it rather than its values.

BEST DESIGNS SO FAR (values already tuned):

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power sensor-node load $R_L$ from a piezo transducer.
    *   Constraints:
        *   $v_{avg} \ge 1.8$ V (S1-S6)
        *   $v_{max} \le 3.6$ V (S1-S6)
        *   $v_{pp} \le 0.05$ V (S1-S6)
        *   $t_{up} \le 0.4$ s (Cold start)
        *   $dv \le 0.02$ V (Stability)
    *   Piezo properties: Sinusoidal current source $I_p$, parallel $C_p$ (25-30 nF), $R_{leak} = 20$ M$\Omega$.
    *   Open-circuit voltage amplitude $V_{oc} \approx 0.76$ V (S1). This is very low, barely enough to overcome diode drops in a standard bridge.

    *   Design `sshi_fbr` (SSHI with Full Bridge Rectifier) is the best so far (Score 65.25).
    *   It uses an SSHI-like inductive stage ($L_1$, $S_1$, $G_1$) and a Full Bridge Rectifier (FBR) ($D_1-D_4$).
    *   Failing points for `sshi_fbr`:
        *   S3, S4: Ripple ($v_{pp}$) is too high.
        *   S4: Settled ($dv$) is too high.
    *   Analysis: High ripple and drift on S4 (weakest excitation, light load) suggest that the storage capacitor $C_1$ is too small to buffer the charge, or the charging is too slow/irregular. However, the $v_{avg}$ is fine.
    *   S4 $v_{avg} = 2.61$ V, $v_{pp} = 86.4$ mV, $dv = 91.3$ mV.
    *   The issue is the storage capacity versus the load. On S4, $R_L = 22$ M$\Omega$. The time constant $\tau = R_L \cdot C_1 \approx 22 \cdot 10^6 \cdot 2.64 \cdot 10^{-7} \approx 5.8$ s. This explains why it hasn't settled by 0.8 s ($dv$ is high).
    *   Increasing $C_1$ would reduce ripple and $dv$, but it would increase $t_{up}$ (startup time).
    *   The existing `sshi_fbr` is already quite good. The problem is simply that $C_1$ is a compromise. If we increase $C_1$ to fix S4 ripple/settled, we might blow $t_{up}$ on S4. Wait, on S4 $t_{up}$ is 0.303 s, which is close to the 0.4 s limit.

    *   The current topology is: Piezo $\rightarrow$ Inductive SSHI $\rightarrow$ Full Bridge $\rightarrow$ Storage Capacitor $\rightarrow$ Load.
    *   Wait, let's look at the components of `sshi_fbr` again:
        *   $L_1, S_1, G_1$ (SSHI inverter)
        *   $D_1, D_2, D_3, D_4$ (Full Bridge)
        *   $C_1$ (Storage)
        *   $DZ_1$ (Zener clamp)
    *   Wait, the FBR diodes $D_1-D_4$ are in parallel with the SSHI?
        *   $D_1$ is pzp to out, $D_2$ is pzn to out, $D_3$ is 0 to pzp, $D_4$ is 0 to pzn.
        *   $L_1$ is pzp to n1, $S_1$ is n1 to pzn.
    *   This means the inductive part flips the charge of $C_p$ and the bridge rectifies it.

    *   To reduce ripple $v_{pp}$ and $dv$, we need more capacitance $C_1$.
    *   But $t_{up}$ on S4 is already 0.303 s. If we increase $C_1$ too much, $t_{up}$ will exceed 0.4 s.
    *   Is there a way to increase the energy transfer efficiency to allow a larger $C_1$ while keeping $t_{up}$ low?
    *   The SSHI efficiency depends on the $L$ and $t_{on}$ values.
    *   Alternatively, we can try a different rectification scheme. A full bridge has two diode drops. A half-bridge or a synchronous rectifier would be better.
    *   Wait, I can use switches $S$ and $SYNC$ controllers for rectification.

    *   Current: SSHI $\rightarrow$ FBR $\rightarrow$ Out.
    *   Better: SSHI $\rightarrow$ Synchronous Rectifier $\rightarrow$ Out.
    *   Since we have a limit of 4 switches and 2 SYNCs:
        *   SYNC1 for SSHI inversion (S1).
        *   SYNC2 for rectification?
    *   But the SSHI itself is a form of rectification/conversion.

    *   Let's look at the "Standard" SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor).
    *   Typically, SSHI uses a switch to connect an inductor across the piezo at the peaks.
    *   Then the current flows through a diode to the storage cap.
    *   The `sshi_fbr` is basically this: $L_1+S_1$ is the inverter, and the FBR is the rectifier.
    *   The FBR has 2 diode drops ($\approx 0.5$ V). With $V_{oc} \approx 0.76$ V, that's a huge loss.
    *   If we use a half-bridge or a more efficient rectifier, we get more voltage.

    *   Instead of a Full Bridge (4 diodes), use a Half Bridge (2 diodes) if the piezo is referenced to ground. But the piezo is $pzp$ and $pzn$.
    *   Let's try a Synchronous Rectifier using the second SYNC.
    *   Wait, if I use $S_1$ for the inversion, and a second switch $S_2$ for the transfer to $C_{out}$.
    *   Proposed Topology (Synchronous SSHI):
        1.  Inductor $L_1$ and Switch $S_1$ (ctrl $G_1$) for charge inversion at the peaks (edges="both").
        2.  A switch $S_2$ (ctrl $G_2$) to transfer the energy to $C_{out}$ at the same peaks?
        3.  No, the current flows through the inductor and then into the cap.
    *   Let's refine the `sshi_fbr` to use a simpler rectifier if possible.
    *   Actually, the `sshi_fbr` is almost there. The problem is S4 ripple and settled.
    *   S4: $v_{avg}=2.61$, $v_{pp}=86$ mV, $dv=91$ mV, $t_{up}=0.303$ s.
    *   If I increase $C_1$ from $2.64 \cdot 10^{-7}$ to $1 \cdot 10^{-6}$, $t_{up}$ might increase to $\approx 0.303 \cdot (1/0.264) \approx 1.1$ s (too slow).
    *   So we need *faster* charging to allow a *larger* $C_1$.

    *   The FBR loses $2 \times V_{diode}$.
    *   What if we use a "Parallel-SSHI" or "Differential-SSHI" or just replace the FBR with a more efficient rectification?
    *   Since the piezo current is $I_p \sin(\omega t)$, the voltage is $V_p \cos(\omega t)$.
    *   The SSHI flips the voltage at the peaks.
    *   If we use $D_1$ from $pzp$ to $out$ and $D_2$ from $pzn$ to $out$, and we tie $pzn$ to a capacitor (or use a floating arrangement), we can reduce the diode drop.
    *   Actually, the simplest way to reduce diode drop is a half-wave rectifier, but that wastes half the energy.
    *   What about a "Synchronous Rectifier"?
        *   $S_1$ (SYNC $G_1$): Connects $L_1$ between $pzp$ and $pzn$ at the peaks (edges="both", phase=0).
        *   $S_2$ (SYNC $G_2$): Connects $pzp$ to $out$ at the positive peak.
        *   $S_3$ (SYNC $G_3$): Connects $pzn$ to $out$ at the negative peak.
        *   This uses 3 switches and 2 SYNCs (since $G_1$ can be "both" and $G_2, G_3$ "pos"/"neg").
        *   Wait, we only have 2 SYNCs.
        *   $G_1$ (edges="both"): $S_1$ (inversion).
        *   $G_2$ (edges="both"): $S_2$ (rectification)? No, that doesn't make sense.
    *   Let's try a different approach: a "Charge Pump" style or an "Inductive Boost".
    *   Wait, the `sshi_fbr` is already an inductive boost. The FBR is the bottleneck.

    *   Instead of a Full Bridge, use a "Half Bridge" with a center-tapped-like configuration? No.
    *   Let's use a "Synchronous Rectifier" with 2 switches and 1 SYNC.
        *   $G_2$ (edges="both", phase=0): $S_2$ connects $pzp$ to $out$ at the positive peak? No, a switch is bidirectional.
        *   If $S_2$ connects $pzp$ to $out$, current flows both ways.
        *   We need diodes to prevent reverse flow.
        *   So: $S_2$ in series with $D_{rect}$.
    *   Actually, let's try to improve the `sshi_fbr` by using a "Symmetric SSHI" (Half-bridge) which is often more efficient.
        *   $S_1$ connects $pzp$ to $n1$, $S_2$ connects $pzn$ to $n1$. No.
        *   The standard SSHI:
            Piezo terminals $pzp, pzn$.
            $S_1$ closes to flip $C_p$ using $L_1$.
            Rectifier $D_1, D_2$ to $out$.
            Wait, if $pzn$ is grounded, we only need one diode $D_1$ from $pzp$ to $out$.
            But $pzn$ is not grounded; it's the other terminal of the piezo.
            If we tie $pzn$ to $0$ through a large capacitor, it becomes a virtual ground.

    *   Let's try this:
        $L_1$ from $pzp$ to $n1$.
        $S_1$ from $n1$ to $pzn$ (ctrl $G_1$).
        $D_1$ from $pzp$ to $out$.
        $D_2$ from $pzn$ to $out$.
        $C_{mid}$ from $pzn$ to $0$ (to stabilize $pzn$ as a reference).
        $C_1$ from $out$ to $0$.
        This is like a "Half-Bridge SSHI". The $D_1, D_2$ are the rectifier.
        Is this better than a Full Bridge?
        FBR: $pzp \to D_1 \to out$, $pzn \to D_2 \to out$, $0 \to D_3 \to pzp$, $0 \to D_4 \to pzn$.
        In the Half-Bridge, the return path is through $C_{mid}$ and the piezo.
        Actually, let's use a more robust SSHI:
        1.  $L_1$ and $S_1$ (SYNC $G_1$, edges="both") across the piezo ($pzp$ to $pzn$).
        2.  Diodes $D_1$ (pzp to out) and $D_2$ (pzn to out).
        3.  A capacitor $C_{mid}$ between $pzn$ and $0$ (or $pzp$ and $0$).
        Wait, if I have $D_1$ and $D_2$ both going to $out$, then the current must return to the piezo. If $pzn$ is tied to $0$, the current returns through $pzn$.
        This is the "Half-Bridge" SSHI. It's known to be more efficient than FBR SSHI because it only has one diode drop in the path.

    *   Let's trace the current:
        - $V(pzp)$ goes high, $D_1$ conducts $\to C_{out}$. Return path is $0 \to pzn$ (via $C_{mid}$).
        - $V(pzp)$ goes low, $D_2$ conducts $\to C_{out}$. Return path is $0 \to pzp$ (via $C_{mid}$).
        - $S_1$ closes at peaks $\to L_1$ flips $C_p$ voltage.
        - Only one diode drop ($V_{out} = V_{piezo} - V_D$).
        - Compare to FBR: $V_{out} = V_{piezo} - 2 V_D$.
        - This should provide more voltage, meaning we can afford a larger $C_1$ to fix the ripple/settled issues on S4.

    *   $L_1$: pzp to n1
    *   $S_1$: n1 to pzn (ctrl $G_1$)
    *   $G_1$: SYNC, edges="both", phase=0, ton=...
    *   $D_1$: pzp to out (DSCH)
    *   $D_2$: pzn to out (DSCH)
    *   $C_{mid}$: pzn to 0 (Value? Maybe 1-10 uF)
    *   $C_1$: out to 0 (Value? 1-10 uF)
    *   $DZ_1$: 0 to out (DZ33)

    *   Wait, if $C_{mid}$ is too small, $pzn$ will bounce. If it's too large, it might slow down the startup.
    *   Let's try $C_{mid} = 1$ uF and $C_1 = 2.2$ uF.

    *   Wait, let's consider another option: a "Synchronous Rectifier" using $S_2$.
        $G_2$ (edges="both", phase=0) closes $S_2$.
        If $S_2$ is from $pzp$ to $out$, it will conduct both ways. We still need a diode.
        $S_2$ in series with $D_1$.
        But a SYNC switch is already very low resistance (2 Ohm).
        The real gain is removing the diode drop. But $S_2$ cannot prevent backflow from $C_{out}$ to the piezo.
        So we must use diodes for the rectifier.

    *   Is the Half-Bridge (with $C_{mid}$) better?
        Yes, it reduces the diode drop from $2 \times 0.25\text{V} = 0.5\text{V}$ to $1 \times 0.25\text{V} = 0.25\text{V}$.
        Given $V_{oc} \approx 0.76$ V, a 0.25 V difference is huge.

    *   What about the $L_1$ and $S_1$ configuration?
        In `sshi_fbr`, it was $L_1$ (pzp-n1), $S_1$ (n1-pzn). This is a series $L-S$ across the piezo.
        Wait, if $L_1$ is in series with $S_1$, the current only flows when $S_1$ is closed.
        This is the standard SSHI.

    *   Let's refine the Half-Bridge SSHI:
        $S_1$: n1 to pzn, ctrl $G_1$ (edges="both")
        $L_1$: pzp to n1
        $D_1$: pzp to out
        $D_2$: pzn to out
        $C_{mid}$: pzn to 0
        $C_1$: out to 0
        $DZ_1$: 0 to out

    *   Wait, let's think about the $C_{mid}$ value. $C_{mid}$ should be larger than $C_p$ to act as a voltage reference.
    *   $C_p = 25\text{--}30$ nF. $C_{mid} = 100$ nF or $1 \mu\text{F}$ should be plenty.
    *   Let's try $C_{mid} = 1 \mu\text{F}$.

    *   $S_1$: n1 to pzn, ctrl $G_1$ (edges="both", phase=0, ton=3e-5)
    *   $L_1$: pzp to n1 (value 2.2 mH)
    *   $D_1$: pzp to out (DSCH)
    *   $D_2$: pzn to out (DSCH)
    *   $C_{mid}$: pzn to 0 (1 uF)
    *   $C_1$: out to 0 (2.2 uF)
    *   $DZ_1$: 0 to out (DZ33)
    *   Total components: 8. (Well within the 16 limit).

    *   S4 failed `settled` and `ripple` because $C_1$ was too small ($2.64 \cdot 10^{-7}$ F).
    *   Wait, the `sshi_fbr` $C_1$ was $0.26 \mu\text{F}$.
    *   With a Half-Bridge, we get more voltage. This might allow us to use a larger $C_1$ while still meeting the $t_{up}$ (startup) requirement.
    *   Let's try $C_1 = 2.2 \mu\text{F}$.
    *   $t_{up}$ is the time to reach 1.8 V.
    *   Energy $E = \frac{1}{2} C V^2$.
    *   For $C_1 = 0.26 \mu\text{F}$ and $V = 1.8\text{V}$, $E \approx 0.42 \mu\text{J}$.
